judge_assessment.explanation: Every mathematical claim the judge makes is correct and I reproduced all of it. h(2) = 5 sin(pi/2) + 9 = 14 and Figure 1 does peak at 14 near t = 2. The amplitude/midline pairs (5, 9), (4, 8) and (8, 10) are right, as is the half-period reasoning that gives period 12 in problems 8 and 9 and B = pi/6. Problem 7: cos(pi t/6) = 0 on 0 <= t < 12 puts pi t/6 in [0, 2pi), so the only solutions are t = 3 and t = 9. Problem 11: cos(pi(t-3)/6) = 1/2 puts the argument in [-pi/2, 3pi/2), so t = 1 and t = 5 and no others — the completeness the judge credits is genuine, not assumed. Problem 12: Ana gives -20 cos(5pi/6) + 23 and Ben gives 20 sin(pi/3) + 23, both 10 sqrt(3) + 23 exactly, and the key's identity sin(theta - pi/2) = -cos theta is the right justification. The tikz/pgfplots figure plots 5*sin(deg(pi*x/4)) + 9 with the degree conversion handled correctly, gridlines at every 2 units, and maxima landing on t = 2 and t = 10 as problem 4 asserts. Where I differ from a 32/32 is one uncovered open-response slot the judge did not count. Problem 11 does not only ask for the solution times — it prints 'There is more than one; explain briefly how the graph tells you how many to expect.' That is an explanation, the key answers it in Step 5 ('y = 10 is a horizontal line above the midline but below the maximum of 12, so it cuts each single cycle exactly twice'), and verify.json id 11 contains a single solve_interval entry with no manual companion. final_response.md's 'What is flagged for manual review' section names only problem 12(b), so the package presents problem 11 as fully machine-covered when its second half is prose. The judge recorded manual_items_reviewed: 1, so that explanation was never reviewed. Related and smaller: problem 12 mixes machine entries with its manual entry, and the Quick Answers row prints '12. 10 sqrt(3) + 23, 10 sqrt(3) + 23' with no marker showing that part (b) still needs a human.

strengths_to_preserve: The interleaving is real rather than nominal. After the Figure 1 warm-up (problems 1-4), the four subskills cycle twice in a different order each time — build (5), evaluate (6), solve (7), build (8), read (9), evaluate (10), solve (11) — so a student cannot carry a method forward from the previous item. That is the structure the prompt asked for and it is executed exactly.

The two Ferris-wheel/harbour contexts are each used across several non-adjacent problems (5 -> 6 -> 7 -> 12 and 8 -> 10 -> 11), so the student builds a model and then has to live with it. Problem 8's model is derived in 8(c) and handed back in 10 and 11 in explicit form, which removes the risk of a cascading error while keeping the continuity.

The degree/radian trap is handled properly: the worksheet directions warn that 'a calculator left in degree mode will return a plausible but wrong number', and the key's common-wrong-answers block gives the actual number it produces — 'about 3.05' for problem 6 — with the observation that it 'looks plausible' because it lands near the bottom of the wheel. Naming the specific plausible-but-wrong value is what makes the warning usable.

Problem 7's grading note states the diagnostic purpose outright: 'an answer of t = 3 alone is the error this problem is built to catch. A horizontal line through the midline cuts one cycle of the curve twice.' Both periodic-equation items (7 and 11) are designed around solution-count completeness rather than around solving mechanics.

Problem 12(b)'s model answer is genuinely well specified: it separates what a graph determines (amplitude, midline, period — 'measurements of the picture and cannot be argued with') from what it does not (C, the sine/cosine choice, and the sign of A, which trade off), and the grading note names the answer to push back on — 'They are both right because they both work'. That is a rubric a second teacher could apply consistently.

Figure 1's pgfplots setup is correct and legible: axis lines=left, ticks every 2 on both axes, a light minor grid at 0.15pt with a heavier major grid at 0.3pt, and a domain of 0:16 that shows two full periods so the peak-to-peak measurement problem 4 asks for is actually performable from the picture.

root_causes.description: Problem 11 carries two responses — the solution set and an explanation of how the graph predicts the solution count — and only the solution set is recorded. Because the item's verify entry is a solve_interval, the package reports it as fully machine-checked and the manual-item count stays at one. The explanation is not incidental: it is the same completeness idea problem 7's grading note calls the error the sheet is built to catch, so the unrecorded half is the conceptual half.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 11: 'Find all times t with 0 <= t < 12 hours at which the harbour depth ... equals 10 feet. There is more than one; explain briefly how the graph tells you how many to expect.'
verify.json id 11: a single {"type": "solve_interval", "expr": "4*cos(pi*(t - 3)/6) + 8 - 10", "var": "t", "expected": [1, 5]} — no manual entry.
answer_key.pdf solution 11 Step 5 supplies the expected explanation in full, so the author wrote the answer without declaring the slot.
final_response.md section 'What is flagged for manual review' names only problem 12(b).

root_causes.description: Problem 12 has both machine entries and a manual entry, and the Quick Answers row shows no sign of the manual half. scripts/render_quick_answers.py render_entry gathers only entries carrying an 'expected' key and reaches the manual em-dash fallback only when that list is empty, so the sheet's single declared manual item is invisible in the fast-grading column.
evidence: verify.json id 12 contains two eval entries plus one manual entry for part (b).
answer_key.pdf Quick Answers row 12 prints the two identical exact values and nothing else.
scripts/render_quick_answers.py render_entry: the '---' fallback is guarded by 'if not vals', unreachable for a mixed problem.

improvements.title: Declare problem 11's solution-count explanation as a manual sub-part alongside its solve_interval entry
improvements.proposed_change: Require that a printed request whose answer is a sentence carries a manual verify entry scoped to that sub-part, even when the same problem also has a fully machine-checked part. Add a lint that scans worksheet prompt text for explanation imperatives ('explain briefly how ...', 'say why ...', 'describe how ...') and fails the gate when the corresponding verify id has no manual entry. Update references/manual-review-aid.md with the periodic-equation pattern specifically: 'find all solutions' is machine-checkable, but 'explain how the graph tells you how many to expect' is not, and the two routinely appear in one item.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture built from curr-420 problem 11: prompt text containing 'explain briefly how the graph tells you how many to expect' with a verify.json id whose only entry is a solve_interval. The gate must exit non-zero naming the unflagged explanation, and must pass once a manual entry for that sub-part is added. Assert also that the reported manual-item count for the fixture rises from 1 to 2.
improvements.expected_impact: Makes the declared manual count honest on a case that currently scores a perfect 32 while shipping an ungraded written response. The mixed 'compute all solutions AND explain the count' shape is common throughout the trigonometry and periodic-modelling band, so the rule generalises.
improvements.risk: Prompt-text scanning will over-trigger on instructional asides that use 'explain' without demanding a written answer, and under-trigger on explanation requests phrased as questions ('why does this happen?'). The lint needs an author-facing override and should be tuned against the existing baseline worksheets before it hard-fails.

improvements.title: Show a manual-review marker on Quick Answers rows that mix machine-verified and manual entries
improvements.proposed_change: Change scripts/render_quick_answers.py render_entry so any problem whose entry list contains a type == 'manual' appends an explicit marker to its bank row, rather than reaching the manual em-dash only when the problem has no machine entries at all. Print a one-line legend under the bank explaining the glyph so a printed key is self-describing.
improvements.regression_test: Render curr-420's verify.json id 12 (two eval entries plus one manual entry) and assert the bank row carries a manual marker. It renders today as the two exact values with no marker, so the assertion fails before the fix. Assert a manual-only problem still renders the plain em-dash so existing behaviour is preserved.
improvements.expected_impact: On this sheet it surfaces the synthesis item — the one problem carrying the assessed reasoning — in the column a teacher grades from. Applies to every worksheet whose final synthesis problem attaches an explanation to a computed value, which is most of the interleaved-synthesis mode.
improvements.risk: Adds width to bank rows and can push the adaptive column count down on dense sheets; a single glyph rather than a word keeps the cost small.

case_summary: An excellent interleaved trigonometric-modelling sheet. The subskills genuinely alternate rather than block, two contexts (Ferris wheel, harbour tide) recur across non-adjacent problems so a built model is reused, and the figure is a correct pgfplots rendering showing two full periods so the peak-to-peak period measurement in problem 4 is actually performable. I recomputed every value independently — including the solution-set completeness in problems 7 and 11 by bounding the argument's range over the given interval — and found no mathematical error; both Ferris-wheel forms agree at 10 sqrt(3) + 23 exactly, and problem 12(b)'s model answer correctly separates the parameters a graph determines from those it does not. The ACCEPT is right and most of the 32/32 is earned. The gap is that problem 11 prints a second, prose response ('explain briefly how the graph tells you how many to expect'), the key answers it, and verify.json records only the solve_interval — so final_response.md flags one manual item when there are two, and the judge reviewed one. Secondarily, problem 12's declared manual part leaves no marker in the Quick Answers bank because the renderer only prints the manual em-dash for problems with no machine entries.
